summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation and hate-propaganda provisions of the Criminal Code, both carried by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in British Columbia, and sexual orientation has been covered federally since 1996. Courts have applied these protections consistently, and no province or territory restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation. It was the first jurisdiction in Canada to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code, in 1992, and it is routinely assessed as the country's most progressive province on LGBT issues; Vancouver's Davie Village remains the established social centre. Provincial human rights machinery is available to visitors and residents who face discrimination, and entry into Canada carries no trans-specific friction.

Legal gender recognition is available across the country. Transgender people may change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, and federal identity documents can carry an X marker. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults. The national baseline equality score of 0.86 rests on Charter equality protection, nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation, and legal gender change in every province including British Columbia.

National crime data gives a mixed picture. A Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in Canada in 2024, up 1% from 2023, which had itself risen 34% from 2022; the total has more than doubled since 2018, an increase of 169%, while the rate per 100,000 population fell 2% to 11.9. Incidents targeting sexual orientation declined 26% to 658, and religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. These figures are national and contain no British Columbia breakdown.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and those held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners in Canadian jails and a heightened risk of sexual assault, while a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns bear on a visitor only if detained.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-provincial policy turbulence is concentrated in schools and sport, and it primarily affects minors and residents rather than visitors. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or to disclose their gender identity at school; human rights groups called for repeal and litigation followed. Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, the Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from legal challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause. British Columbia is not among the provinces pursuing this line of legislation.

Comparative positioning matters when reading British Columbia against the rest of Canada. The province was the first jurisdiction in the country to write sexual orientation into its human-rights code and is routinely ranked as the most progressive province on LGBT issues, while the national baseline score of 0.86 already reflects Charter equality protection and nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation. Two other provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, are the reference points for the direction of travel in education and sport policy.

The national hate-crime trend runs in two directions at once: overall police-reported incidents rose 1% in 2024 after a 34% jump the previous year and are up 169% since 2018, while the sexual-orientation category fell 26%. A visitor weighing Vancouver against other Canadian cities should note that the dataset is national and does not isolate either gender identity or British Columbia.
localsOnly:
British Columbia residents had the first statutory route in Canada to recognition of sexual orientation in a human-rights code, through the 1992 amendment, and the provincial human rights machinery remains the standing complaint route for discrimination on the protected grounds of gender identity and gender expression.

Residents change the gender marker on official documents through a provincial route whose rules vary between provinces and territories, alongside federal identity documents that can carry an X marker. The provincial rules for British Columbia specifically are not set out in the available sources.

The live domestic policy disputes sit in schools and in sport, where parental-consent requirements for gender-related names and identity and restrictions on participation have been legislated in two other provinces and defended with the notwithstanding clause. These measures govern residents and minors, not visitors passing through.

For residents in custody, federal policy places transgender prisoners according to gender identity and requires consideration of sex-reassignment surgery after 12 continuous months of detention, with the Kavanagh litigation the worked example of enforcement.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada release of 30 March 2026 reports no British Columbia breakdown, so the volume and direction of hate crime in this province is unresolved. The dataset breaks out sexual orientation as a motivation category rather than gender identity, so trans-specific hate-crime volume is not established by this source either.

Egale Canada has published an analysis report on 2024 police-reported hate-crime incidents affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada, but its province-level and trans-specific findings are not sourced in the available inventory and are not reproduced here.

Enforcement of the nationwide conversion-therapy ban inside British Columbia is not sourced. No British Columbia prosecutions, complaints or court decisions are documented in the available material, so the practical reach of the 2021 amendment in this province remains unresolved.

The corrections findings are drawn from federal policy, one litigation case and one 2022 study of correctional officers in Nova Scotia. Conditions in British Columbia's own provincial institutions are not sourced, and no trans-specific assault or discrimination figures for this province are available.

The national baseline equality score of 0.86 is cited without its methodology, weighting or date of assessment in the available sources, so its composition beyond the three stated components is unresolved.
